ta-l1d43q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 43 turns to the necessity of divine operation and announces two articles: whether God acts by necessity of nature, and whether by necessity of his justice.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that God acts by necessity of nature. Dionysius says as our sun, not reasoning or choosing, pours its rays on all bodies, so divine goodness on all beings, and acting without reasoning and choice is acting by necessity of nature.
claims: God acts like the sun.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e115.summary: Second argument. Every agent acting by its essence acts by necessity of nature, since what follows an essence as such necessarily follows it, and God acts by his essence as first agent.
claims: Acting by essence is acting by nature.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e118.summary: Third argument. As God is good per se, he is necessary being per se, all things having necessity from him, and in the per se good there is only good, so in the per se necessary there is only necessity, and his operation is necessary.
claims: The necessary being acts necessarily.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e122.summary: Fourth argument. The cause of the necessary must be necessary, and all beings are created by divine operation, so if it were not necessary, nothing would be necessary, against sense and all science.
claims: Necessary effects need a necessary cause.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e125.summary: Sed contra. From one agent acting by necessity of nature comes only one thing, since the same always makes the same, so only one thing would come immediately from God and others from it, against the faith confessing God creator of all and no other creator.
claims: Natural necessity yields only one effect.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e128.summary: Second sed contra. Every natural agent produces an effect coeval with itself unless impeded, and God's infinite power cannot be impeded, so he would have created a world coeternal with himself, against the faith.
claims: Natural necessity yields a coeternal world.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever is by necessity of nature is either intended or ordered to an end or not. If not, it is by chance, which is nature acting beside its intention (Physics 2), as monsters arise by the necessity of a particular nature though ordered to an end by universal nature. God cannot act so, or all things would happen by chance, as by necessity of matter, and no nature would intend an end, against the Philosopher, since a created nature intends an end only as ordered by its cause. If ordered to an end, this is by a separate orderer or a conjoined one. By a separate orderer, natural operations tend certainly to their ends by the provision and ordering of such a cause, so Themistius says nature acts as if moved by higher causes, with an instinct from the ordering of separate substances. God's works cannot be so ordered, since something prior to God would direct his work to its end. So what he does by the power of his nature is ordered to an end by an orderer joined to him, his wisdom, so his works proceed from the order of his wisdom and so from his will, which loves that order, not by necessity of nature. This appears especially in the arrangement of the heavens, the number and distances of stars and sizes of orbs, for which no reason can be given except the order of the creator's wisdom, though some diversity among generables may be explained by matter, which is why the Lord in Scripture often points to the heavens to show his divinity (Isa. 40:26, 'lift up your eyes and see who created these').
claims: God does not act by necessity of nature but by the order of his wisdom and his will.
Natural agents are ordered to ends by a higher intelligence; God by his own wisdom.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the first argument. Dionysius likens divine goodness to the visible sun not as to necessity of acting but as to universality of causing, as appears from his showing its rays reaching the lowest beings.
claims: The sun analogy concerns universality, not necessity.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e140.summary: Reply to the second argument. As will, essence, and wisdom are really one in God but conceptually distinct, so operations are distinguished by the attributes' concepts, though his operation is one, his essence. Creation, though an operation of his essence, is so not only as essence but as wisdom and will, so it follows the condition of knowledge and will, and since will is free, God makes things by freedom of will, not necessity of nature.
claims: Creation follows the condition of will, which is free.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e144.summary: Reply to the third argument. Whatever is in God is his essence, so all is eternal, uncreated, and necessary, but the effect of his operation does not proceed necessarily, since it proceeds from the operation as from the will, and so according to the will's freedom.
claims: What is in God is necessary; his effects are free.
concepts: necessity in God vs. freedom of effects

ta-l1d43q2-d1e147.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God's will or operation should not be called contingent, since contingency implies mutability, which is not in God, but there is freedom of will and operation as it goes out from the will.
claims: God's will is free, not contingent.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e159.summary: First argument that God acts by necessity of justice. The Gloss on 2 Tim. 2:13, 'he cannot deny himself', says he would deny himself if he abandoned his justice, which is himself.
claims: God cannot abandon his justice.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e165.summary: Second argument. Whatever is not just, if done, is done unjustly, and God cannot do anything unjustly, or he could sin.
claims: God cannot act unjustly.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e168.summary: Third argument. Natural causes act by necessity because determined to one, and God's will is immutably determined to justice.
claims: God's will is determined to justice.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e172.summary: Sed contra from the Gloss on Jonah 2: the merciful God is ready to save by mercy those he cannot save by justice.
claims: God saves by mercy beyond justice.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e178.summary: Second sed contra. Saving those in hell is not of justice but against it, yet, as is read, at Gregory's prayers the Lord recalled from hell and restored to life the emperor Trajan, an idolater damned for it.
claims: Trajan was recalled from hell.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e181.summary: Third sed contra. If he can act only by justice, this is created justice, which does not regulate what is, or uncreated justice, which does not oppose his power or will.
claims: Neither justice constrains God.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e184.summary: Thomas's determination. 'God acts by necessity of justice' can mean that he can do nothing that would not be just if done, which is true, as he can do nothing that would not be willed or known by him; or that his justice determines him to do one thing so that he cannot do another, which is false. When the whole determination of the work is from the operator, it is in him to determine this or that; when the work is determined of itself, it is not further up to him. In human works some things are indifferent of their nature, like sitting or not sitting, and either is made virtuous by the agent applying due circumstances, so justice compels neither, and whichever he does will be just with due circumstances by the order of reason; others are determined to one by their form, like lying, evil in itself, or keeping the equality of justice, good in itself, which we cannot neglect or do without injustice. Whatever is ordered, just, or good in created things is wholly from God's ordering will, so he does not do this by necessity of justice so as to be unable to do another, since he could place the same mode of order on something else: as his knowledge causes created truths, unlike ours, his just will causes just things, so if he did something else, he would make it just and would not be unjust.
claims: God can do nothing that would be unjust if done, but justice does not determine him to one course.
God's will causes what is just in creatures, as his knowledge causes created truths.
concepts: divine will as source of created justice

ta-l1d43q2-d1e187.summary: Reply to the first argument. Justice can be taken as the ordering of the divine will in God, and he cannot act beyond it any more than beyond his knowledge; or as the justice determined in a caused work by the order of his will, and beyond that he can act without denying himself, since in what he did the order of his justice would appear, so he would act neither against justice nor unjustly.
claims: God can act beyond determined created justice but not beyond his own ordering.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e194.summary: Reply to the third argument. Though God's will is immutably determined to justice, the order of justice is not determined to this or that thing, so he does not do this or that by necessity of justice.
claims: Justice is not determined to particular things.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e197.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. Justice is said of God two ways: as retribution for merits, corresponding to particular justice, which regards equality and order on the side of things, and God sometimes passes over this, his work proceeding by mercy; and as the fittingness of divine goodness, corresponding to general justice in politics, the common virtue (the Philosopher), which regards order on God's side, and God never acts nor can act beyond it, since he can do nothing unfitting to himself. Liberality, giving someone what is not due, does not conflict with this justice, and this is God's mercy, by which he infuses grace even into sinners worthy of death that they may be worthy of life, placing another order in the thing, so that what was ordered by fault to punishment is ordered by grace to glory.
claims: God may pass over retributive justice but never the justice of his goodness's fittingness.
Mercy is liberality consistent with God's justice.
concepts: iustitia as retribution vs. decentia bonitatis

ta-l1d43q2-d1e200.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Trajan, perhaps raised after five hundred years, and others raised after one day were not finally damned, since God foreknew they would be freed from punishment by the saints' prayers and restored to life, and so by the liberality of his goodness he pardoned them though they deserved eternal punishment. God, against whom alone sin is committed, differs from another judge, so he can freely remit without offending anyone, unlike a judge who must punish a fault against another, the commonwealth, or God, and so cannot lawfully remit the punishment.
claims: Trajan was not finally damned; God can remit what is offence against himself alone.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e203.summary: Reply to the third sed contra. God is said unable to act unjustly not because his justice opposes his power but because of incompossibility: that God does something and it is not just are incompossible.
claims: God's acting and injustice are incompossible.

ta-l1d43q2-d1e212.summary: An expositio textus. Lombard's solution: in 'God can do only what is just', 'just' can be joined first with 'is', which restricts it to the present, making the sense 'God can do only what is now just', which is false, since he can make things that are nothing now; or first with 'can', which has ampliating force, so 'just' supposes for an indeterminate present, not a determinate time, meaning 'God cannot do anything that would not be just whenever he did it', which is true, and this solves all the objections.
claims: 'God can do only what is just' is true with ampliation by 'can', false restricted to the present.

ta-l1d43q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two articles on the necessity of divine operation: by nature and by justice.

ta-l1d43q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that God does not act by necessity of nature, since natural agents are ordered to ends by a higher intelligence, and God's works are ordered by his own wisdom and so proceed from his will, which loves that order. This appears in the arrangement of the heavens. Creation follows the condition of free will, what is in God is necessary but his effects free, and his will is free without being contingent.
claims: God creates by wisdom and free will, not natural necessity.

ta-l1d43q2-Dd1e151.summary: Article 2 holds that God can do nothing that would be unjust if done, but justice does not determine him to one course, since his will causes what is just in creatures. He may pass over retributive justice by mercy but never the justice of his goodness's fittingness. Trajan was not finally damned, and God can remit offences against himself.
claims: God is not bound by necessity of justice to one course; mercy is consistent with his justice.

ta-l1d43q2-Dd1e207.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 43 explains Lombard's solution by ampliation: God cannot do anything that would not be just whenever done, though he can do what is not now just.
claims: 'Just' ampliated by 'can' makes the proposition true.

ta-l1d43q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 43 treats necessity in God's operation. Article 1 holds that God does not act by necessity of nature but by the order of his wisdom and his free will, as shown in the arrangement of the heavens. Article 2 holds that he can do nothing unjust, yet justice does not determine him to one course, since his will is the source of created justice and his mercy is consistent with the justice of his goodness.
claims: God creates freely, not by natural necessity.
God's justice does not bind him to one course; mercy accords with it.
